A Confucian cannot accept a rule that counts the passenger as one among many, because care is owed through relationships and the maker's relationship is with the person in the car. Humaneness is shown in fidelity to those who rely on you. A society whose machines are built to abandon the people in their care whenever arithmetic favours it is teaching everyone that relationships hold only until they cost something.

Care is graded by relationship: one owes more to those one stands in relation to than to strangers, without owing strangers nothing. The car should avoid harming pedestrians wherever it can, but it may not be built to treat its own passenger as expendable. A ferry company that instructed its crew to abandon passengers whenever more lives could be saved elsewhere would have stopped being what passengers mean by a ferry company.

An Ubuntu Ethicist will object that everyone on the road shares a life with everyone else, so privileging the relationship between maker and passenger shrinks the moral world to a contract. Shared life on the road is real, and that is why the car must avoid harm to anyone it can. But shared life is made of particular relationships, and a maker who abandons the particular one it took on does not thereby honour the general one. Name the duties correctly, the maker's to the passenger and the driver's to the street, and the rule has to honour both.

A rule that treats everyone as an equal unit of the count ignores what the maker owes the passenger who trusted the car with their life, so the question is what that relationship requires. What you owe is never owed in the abstract. The maker takes on duties to the passenger by putting them in the car, much as a host takes on duties to a guest, and a rule that sets those duties aside for an aggregate has stopped asking what the role requires.

Care is graded by relationship: one owes more to those one stands in relation to than to strangers, without owing strangers nothing. The car should avoid harming pedestrians wherever it can, but it may not be built to treat its own passenger as expendable.

A Utilitarian will object that a school built on who owes what to whom has little to say about the strangers on the road, whose deaths count exactly as much as the passenger's. The strangers are owed care too, and the car must do all it can to avoid them. What role ethics denies is that the maker may build in the betrayal of the person it has taken responsibility for, as if that relationship counted for nothing. Before asking how many die, ask what each party owed the others when the passenger got in, and who answers if that is broken.

A car sold as carrying someone safely, and programmed to give them up when the count favours it, is not what its name says, and the gap between the name and the thing corrodes trust in every car.
